title: AI Essentials for Everyday Work
subject: Using generative AI for common workplace tasks.

objectiveEvidence.objective: Understand: Explain two useful applications and two limitations of generative AI in everyday workplace tasks.
Apply: Write a prompt that includes a task, relevant context, constraints, and a desired output format.
: Revise an AI-generated workplace message using focused follow-up instructions to meet specified tone and length requirements.
Compare two AI-generated summaries with the original meeting notes and identify unsupported claims, missing details, and altered meanings.
Identify personal or confidential information in a sample prompt and determine what requires removal or authorization before use.
Assess an AI-generated response against accuracy, relevance, completeness, and privacy criteria, then justify whether to use, revise, or reject it.

sources.title: SME source S1
sources.reference: Generative AI creates responses based on patterns learned during training and the context provided to it. It can help draft emails, summarize notes, brainstorm ideas, and organize information. It can also produce incorrect, incomplete, biased, or invented information. A confident tone does not prove accuracy.

sources.title: SME source S2
sources.reference:
A useful prompt includes:
- Task: What should the AI do?
- Context: What background information does it need?
- Constraints: What must it include, avoid, or preserve?
- Output format: How should the response be presented?
For example, “Summarize this” is vague. A clearer instruction is: “Summarize the meeting notes below in five bullet points. Separate confirmed decisions, open questions, and action items. Use only the supplied notes. Mark missing owners or deadlines as ‘Needs clarification.’”

sources.title: SME source S3
sources.reference: Improve responses through focused follow-up instructions. Examples include “Make the language simpler,” “Remove claims not supported by the notes,” and “Separate decisions from suggestions.” Follow-up instructions can improve a response but do not guarantee correctness.

sources.title: SME source S4
sources.reference:
Before using an AI-generated response:
1. Compare it with the original information.
2. Check important facts, names, dates, and calculations.
3. Identify unsupported claims and missing details.
4. Check whether it follows the requested format and tone.
5. Review it for sensitive information.
6. Decide whether to use, revise, or reject it.
Follow organizational policies when using AI tools. Do not enter personal, confidential, or sensitive information unless the tool and intended use are authorized. Use fictional or appropriately anonymized examples during this course.

sources.title: SME source S5
sources.reference: Case study: A team needs a launch-readiness summary. Its meeting notes say: “The launch date is proposed for 18 November but is not approved. Maya will draft the customer email by 12 November. The support checklist needs an owner. The next review is on 14 November.”

sources.title: SME source S6
sources.reference: An acceptable summary must preserve the proposed status of the launch date, assign only the customer-email task to Maya, and flag the missing support-checklist owner. A response that describes the launch date as confirmed or assigns the checklist to Maya introduces unsupported information.

sources.title: SME source S7
sources.reference: For the guided mini project, provide a ready-made, read-only meeting-assistant workflow. Learners run a vague-prompt example and a structured-prompt example, inspect the responses, and explain their differences. Learners must not build or edit the workflow. Clearly label prerecorded or simulated responses; do not present them as live model output.

modules.title: Module 1: Understand AI and write better prompts

problemHook.title: The notes you need to summarize
problemHook.situation:
The notes you need to summarize: Launch proposed for 18 November; not approved. Maya drafts the customer email by 12 November. Support checklist: owner missing. Next review: 14 November.
The draft changes the meaning: Launch date: proposed, not approved. Checklist owner: not recorded.
What would you challenge before sharing?: Which two claims changed? What could a colleague misunderstand? Learn to request a bounded, reviewable draft.
problemHook.question: What should you check before trusting an AI response?

slides.title: Start with a task AI can assist with
body: Draft from supplied talking points.
Summarize a bounded set of notes.
Organize information into a useful format.
Takeaway: Organize information into a useful format.
slides.narration: Generative AI can help create a first draft, condense a set of notes, or reorganize information. Those are three related activities, but they ask for different results. A draft creates wording for you to review. A summary selects and shortens information from a source. An organized task list changes the structure so that actions are easier to see. Start by naming the result you need. For example, a fictional coordinator has approved talking points for a project update. Asking for a draft email gives the assistant a concrete writing task. Asking it to make the project successful does not identify a clear output. The useful contribution here is help with language and organization. You remain responsible for deciding whether the result accurately represents the supplied information. Notice that we have chosen a bounded task with material to work from, rather than asking the assistant to make an unsupported decision.

slides.title: Give the assistant material to work from
body: Source notes provide the content.
The requested output provides the structure.
A draft is a starting point for review.
Takeaway: A draft is a starting point for review.
Practice: Pause for the two midpoint questions.
slides.narration: Now compare two everyday requests. In the first, someone asks for an email about a meeting without providing the decisions. In the second, the person supplies the actual talking points and asks for a concise update. The second request gives the assistant relevant material to transform. That does not guarantee a correct answer, but it makes the intended task clearer. The same distinction applies to summaries. If your source says that a launch date is proposed, that status belongs in the summary. A shorter version should preserve the meaning, not simply produce a more decisive sentence. When organizing a task list, the assistant can present recorded tasks in a table. An absent owner is still absent information; a table cell is not permission to fill the gap with a plausible name. These examples show both the benefit and the boundary of assistance: useful formatting and wording must remain connected to the material you supplied.

slides.title: Choose a useful first task
body: Choose a familiar, bounded task.
Use fictional or authorized information.
Decide how you will check the draft.
Takeaway: Decide how you will check the draft.
slides.narration: A sensible first task is one you understand well enough to review. You might ask for a clearer version of an internal announcement, a summary of fictional meeting notes, or an outline based on supplied project information. Before sending the prompt, decide what a useful result would contain. For the announcement, that could mean keeping the original meaning while simplifying the language. For the summary, it could mean separating decisions from open questions. For a task list, it could mean showing only recorded tasks and identifying missing details. This gives you a basis for review instead of judging only whether the response sounds professional. Use fictional examples in this course, and follow your organization's policy when working with real information. The main idea is straightforward: identify a specific writing or organizing task, supply the relevant material, and retain a clear way to check the result.

questions.hint: Look for a named writing task and supplied material, rather than a broad goal.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which request defines a bounded AI task?
choices: Make our project successful.
Draft an email from these notes.
Decide every team priority.
questions.explanation: Drafting from supplied notes names both an action and material. The alternatives leave the outcome broad or delegate unsupported decisions.

questions.hint: Smooth language tells you about readability. The original notes provide the evidence for accuracy.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. A summary reads smoothly. What should you do next?
choices: Share it without further checks.
Treat fluency as proof of accuracy.
Compare its claims with the notes.
questions.explanation: Readable language does not establish accuracy. Compare the summary with the source before using it.

slides.title: How a fluent answer can be wrong
body: Responses follow learned patterns and supplied context.
Confident wording does not establish accuracy.
An answer can be incomplete or invented.
Takeaway: An answer can be incomplete or invented.
slides.narration: Generative AI produces responses using patterns learned during training and the context available to it. It does not follow that every sentence it produces is a verified statement about your situation. A response may be incomplete, incorrect, biased, or invented. The difficulty for a reader is that a mistake can arrive in the same fluent language as a correct explanation. For example, a summary might say that a team confirmed a launch date when the notes describe it only as proposed. The sentence is easy to read, yet its meaning has changed. Do not use confidence of tone as your accuracy check. Instead, ask what evidence supports each important statement. In a summary task, your immediate reference is the source notes. A familiar-sounding detail should still be checked if it affects a decision, a task, or the status of an agreement.

slides.title: Spot the change in meaning
body: Source: launch date is proposed, not approved.
Faulty summary: launch date is confirmed.
The extra certainty is unsupported.
Takeaway: The extra certainty is unsupported.
Practice: Pause for the two midpoint questions.
slides.narration: Look closely at the fictional launch-readiness example. The notes say that the launch date is proposed for eighteen November and is not approved. A faulty summary says, the launch is confirmed for eighteen November. The date matches, but the status does not. Checking only names and numbers would miss the error. You must also check words that express certainty, responsibility, and agreement. The notes also say that Maya will draft the customer email by twelve November, while the support checklist needs an owner. Assigning the checklist to Maya would introduce another unsupported detail. A person's appearance elsewhere in the notes is not evidence that they own every task. The correct response preserves the proposed status and labels the missing owner for clarification. We are not asking the assistant to make the record sound complete; we are asking it to represent the record faithfully.

slides.title: Set a boundary and keep the review
body: Restrict the answer to supplied information.
Mark missing information explicitly.
Check the response even after a clearer prompt.
Takeaway: Check the response even after a clearer prompt.
slides.narration: You can reduce ambiguity by telling the assistant to use only the supplied notes and mark missing details as needs clarification. These instructions describe the boundary of the task. They do not turn generation into a guarantee of correctness. After receiving a response, compare its important claims with the source. Did a suggestion become a decision? Did an unassigned action gain an owner? Did a proposed date become a commitment? If you find a problem, give a focused correction such as, keep the launch date described as proposed because approval is not recorded. A follow-up can improve the response, but the revised version still needs checking. Later modules will develop that review process in more detail. For now, remember two limitations: a response can introduce unsupported information, and it can omit information you needed. Clear instructions and careful review address different parts of the problem; both matter.

questions.hint: Compare proposed with confirmed. The date can stay the same while the level of certainty changes.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. The source calls a date proposed; the summary calls it confirmed. What changed?
choices: The level of certainty changed.
The calendar date was removed.
The original meaning was retained.
questions.explanation: The same date can carry a different meaning when proposed becomes confirmed. The certainty was not supported by the notes.

questions.hint: A missing owner is a gap in the record, not an invitation to assign the task to someone nearby.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. The checklist has no recorded owner. Which output preserves the source?
choices: Assign it to the email owner.
Mark its owner Needs clarification.
Remove the task from the summary.
questions.explanation: Missing ownership should remain explicit. Assigning an owner invents a fact; removing the task hides an unresolved action.

videos.title: Write a task, context, constraints and format

slides.title: Build a four-part prompt
body: Task: state the action.
Context: supply relevant material.
Constraints: set boundaries.
Format: describe the output.
Takeaway: Format: describe the output.
slides.narration: A practical prompt has four parts: task, context, constraints, and output format. The task states the action, such as summarize the meeting notes. Context provides the material or background needed for that action. Constraints explain what must be preserved, included, or avoided. Output format describes how the response should be organized. Consider the request, summarize this. It names a broad action but leaves several choices open. It does not say whether you need a paragraph, an action table, or a list of decisions. It does not explain how to handle missing information. A structured prompt makes those choices visible. You do not need special technical language. Write ordinary instructions that someone could inspect and understand. The purpose of the four-part structure is to make your intended result clear enough to request and clear enough to review afterward.

slides.title: Turn a vague request into clear instructions
body: Task: summarize these meeting notes.
Constraint: use only the supplied information.
Format: decisions, questions, actions.
Missing owners or dates: Needs clarification.
Takeaway: Missing owners or dates: Needs clarification.
Practice: Pause for the two midpoint questions.
slides.narration: Let us improve the vague request one part at a time. First, name the task: summarize the meeting notes below. Next, supply the notes as the context, rather than expecting the assistant to know what happened. Add a constraint: use only the supplied information and preserve whether a date is proposed or confirmed. Then specify the format: separate confirmed decisions, open questions, and action items. Finally, explain how to represent a gap: label a missing owner or deadline as needs clarification. That last instruction is a constraint, while the three headings describe the format. The distinction helps you diagnose an incomplete prompt. A prompt can have clear headings but still lack rules about unsupported information. It can also have good boundaries but request no useful structure. Together, the four parts describe both the work to perform and the form of the result you intend to check.

slides.title: Check your prompt before using it
body: Can someone identify the requested task?
Is the necessary context included?
Are important boundaries explicit?
Does the format fit the task?
Takeaway: Does the format fit the task?
slides.narration: Before using a prompt, read it as if you were receiving the request for the first time. Can you identify the action to take? Is the necessary source material present? Are there important boundaries that the reader would otherwise have to guess? Is the requested format useful for the person who will receive the result? For example, a short update might need a paragraph, while an action list might need columns for task, owner, and deadline. Avoid adding requirements simply to make the prompt longer. Each instruction should help define the task or prevent a relevant misunderstanding. If the first response misses the requested structure, you can give a focused follow-up that names the specific change. Keep the underlying facts and constraints intact. You now have a repeatable method: state the task, supply context, set meaningful constraints, request a usable format, and review what comes back.

questions.hint: Format describes how information is organized; constraints describe what the response must preserve or avoid.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which instruction specifies an output format?
choices: Use only the supplied notes.
Mark missing owners explicitly.
Separate decisions and actions.
questions.explanation: Separate decisions and actions describes organization. The other instructions set boundaries for the content.

questions.hint: Check whether the prompt says what to do with information not present in the notes.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. A prompt includes a task, notes and headings. What should you check for next?
choices: Boundaries for unsupported details.
Extra words to lengthen the prompt.
A promise of a flawless response.
questions.explanation: The prompt still needs relevant constraints. Extra length is not a goal, and wording cannot guarantee a flawless response.

body: Which two claims changed?

Learn to request a bounded, reviewable draft.
Takeaway: Request a useful draft without changing what the notes say.
hook.narration: Which statements would you challenge before sharing this update? A colleague could mistake a proposal for an agreement or an invented assignment for a real task. This module connects useful AI assistance with its limitations, then shows you how to write clearer instructions.

worked.title: Worked example: choose the evidence

modules.title: Module 2: Use AI for everyday tasks

problemHook.title: The Unapproved Launch Date
problemHook.situation:
The Unapproved Launch Date: A team needs a launch-readiness summary. Meeting notes state the launch date is proposed for 18 November but is not approved.
Spotting the AI Hallucination: AI Draft: 'The launch is confirmed for November 18.' Source Notes: 'Proposed for 18 November but is not approved.'
Why Rigorous Review Matters: Drafting messages and summarizing notes require active oversight. Focused follow-up instructions correct AI errors.
problemHook.question: What should you check before trusting an AI response?

slides.title: Drafting Workplace Messages
body: Translate bullet points into professional emails.
Establish clear tone and appropriate length from the start.
Takeaway: AI accelerates drafting when given clear parameters.
Practice: Review message drafting principles.
slides.narration: Let us explore our first core topic: drafting workplace messages. Generative AI excels at translating raw talking points into polished professional emails or announcements. However, relying on a single initial prompt rarely yields a perfect result. We must understand how to shape tone, adjust length, and ensure that our initial instructions match our professional communication standards before sharing drafts with colleagues or clients. A common misconception is that AI knows your company's preferred communication style automatically, but in reality, you must provide explicit constraints regarding tone and format to avoid overly informal or verbose outputs. Taking time to establish these parameters upfront saves valuable revision cycles later in your workflow.

slides.title: Using Focused Follow-Up Instructions
body: Apply targeted commands like 'Make language simpler.'
Instruct AI to remove unsupported claims explicitly.
Takeaway: Targeted follow-ups refine draft quality efficiently.
Practice: Examine follow-up command patterns.
slides.narration: When an AI draft misses the mark on tone or length, broad commands are rarely effective. Instead, we use focused follow-up instructions to guide the tool toward our exact communication goals. For example, if a fictional project team named Apex Logistics receives an overly complex draft summarizing their latest strategy session, the user can apply targeted commands such as 'Make the language simpler' or 'Remove claims not supported by the notes.' These precise interventions help align the text with specific workplace requirements. Imagine a draft that accidentally mixes up suggestions with finalized budget approvals; a follow-up instruction can request that decisions and suggestions be separated, though the revision still needs checking. Keep in mind that while follow-up instructions significantly improve a response, they do not guarantee absolute factual correctness, which is why your final human review remains indispensable.

slides.title: Iterative Refinement
body: The process of progressively shaping an AI response through targeted follow-up prompts.
Takeaway: Iteration is a normal part of working with AI.
Practice: Note the definition of iterative refinement.
slides.narration: To wrap up our first topic, let us define iterative refinement. It is the deliberate process of progressively shaping an AI response through targeted follow-up prompts rather than accepting the initial output. Consider how the Apex Logistics team handles their weekly status updates: instead of rewriting a messy AI-generated report entirely from scratch, they apply a sequence of focused corrections to polish the draft. By treating AI output as a rough draft requiring editorial oversight, professionals retain responsibility for their communications and may save time on initial drafting. Understanding this iterative cycle prevents frustration and supports clearer messages when people check the final result against the source and intended audience.

questions.hint: Think about how targeted commands address specific flaws.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. What is the primary benefit of using focused follow-up instructions instead of broad commands like 'fix this'?
choices: They guarantee 100 percent factual accuracy in every output.
They target specific tone, length, or content issues for precise improvement.
They eliminate the need for any human review of AI drafts.
questions.explanation: Focused follow-up instructions target specific parameters like tone and length, though they do not guarantee factual correctness.

questions.hint: Recall the definition of iterative refinement from the lesson.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which of the following best describes iterative refinement when drafting messages with AI?
choices: Accepting the first generated response without changes.
Progressively shaping the response through targeted follow-up prompts.
Rewriting the entire email manually from scratch every time.
questions.explanation: Iterative refinement is the progressive shaping of an AI response through targeted follow-up prompts.

slides.title: Summarizing Meeting Notes
body: Condense lengthy discussions into actionable takeaways.
Separate confirmed decisions, open questions, and action items.
Takeaway: Structured summarization prevents critical details from getting lost.
Practice: Review meeting summarization best practices.
slides.narration: Our second topic focuses on summarizing meeting notes effectively. Lengthy transcripts or disorganized discussions can easily overwhelm busy teams. Generative AI can rapidly condense these materials, but only if you instruct it to organize information into logical categories such as confirmed decisions, open questions, and action items. For instance, suppose the Apex Logistics team meets to discuss an upcoming product rollout where a launch date is proposed for eighteen November but remains unapproved, and Maya is assigned to draft a customer email by twelve November. A structured prompt asks the AI to preserve these nuances, but the response still needs checking. A common pitfall is allowing the tool to blend speculation with documented outcomes, treating a proposed date as a confirmed fact. Our summaries must strictly reflect the actual recorded status without assuming unapproved consensus.

slides.title: Preserving Uncertainty and Nuance
body: Maintain conditional language for unapproved items.
Flag missing owners and unassigned deadlines clearly.
Takeaway: Never upgrade tentative statements into confirmed facts.
Practice: Analyze how to handle ambiguity in summaries.
slides.narration: When summarizing notes, preserving nuance is critical. If a deadline is proposed but not approved, the summary must explicitly state that provisional status. Consider a fictional product launch meeting where a release date of November eighteenth is discussed but left unapproved. A reliable summary must maintain this exact uncertainty rather than upgrading the tentative date into a confirmed milestone. Similarly, when action items lack assigned owners or specific due dates, the AI should be instructed to mark them clearly as needs clarification rather than inventing names or dates to fill gaps. Preserving this uncertainty protects the team from acting on false assumptions and maintains accountability across projects. Ignoring missing details or fabricating owners creates severe operational risks that undermine team trust, making strict source adherence an absolute necessity for every generated professional summary.

slides.title: Source Fidelity
body: The degree to which an AI summary accurately reflects source material without adding invented facts.
Takeaway: High source fidelity ensures trustworthy summaries.
Practice: Note the definition of source fidelity.
slides.narration: We conclude our second topic with the vital concept of source fidelity. This refers to the degree to which an AI summary accurately reflects the underlying source material without introducing invented facts, altered statuses, or unauthorized assumptions. For instance, if meeting notes state that Maya will draft a customer email by November twelfth while the support checklist remains unowned, a high-fidelity summary must strictly reflect those exact boundaries. Maintaining high source fidelity is the primary responsibility of the human reviewer when working with generative AI tools. By checking every claim against original notes, you can identify discrepancies before considering the summary for leadership review or distribution, preventing the spread of subtle inaccuracies that often hide behind the confident tone typical of modern generative text models.

questions.hint: Recall the discussion on preserving uncertainty and nuance.

questions.explanation: Source fidelity requires preserving conditional uncertainty rather than upgrading tentative plans into confirmed facts.

slides.title: Organizing Action Plans
body: Transform unstructured project briefs into structured task lists.
Group tasks by milestone, priority, or assigned department.
Takeaway: Structured organization turns vague briefs into executable plans.
Practice: Review action plan organization strategies.
slides.narration: Our third topic explores organizing information into clear action plans. Project briefs often contain narrative descriptions rather than concrete tasks, making it difficult for teams to track deliverables. Generative AI can parse these documents to extract action items, sequence them logically, and format them into tables or bulleted lists. For example, a chaotic project brief for a new mobile application can be transformed into a categorized task list separating design milestones from engineering requirements. However, a common mistake is trusting the AI automated categorization without verifying whether all necessary constraints from the brief were captured. You must actively check that no vital steps were omitted during the restructuring process and that every category aligns perfectly with project objectives, ensuring your team executes only verified and accurately organized operational plans.

slides.title: Verifying Completeness and Owners
body: Check that every task has a verified owner and timeline.
Identify missing responsibilities before sharing plans.
Takeaway: Verification prevents orphan tasks and missed deadlines.
Practice: Examine completeness verification techniques.
slides.narration: When generative AI organizes an action plan, it can produce incorrect, incomplete, biased, or invented information, and a confident tone does not prove accuracy. Imagine a team reviewing a launch-readiness summary where meeting notes state the support checklist needs an owner. If the AI confidently assigns Maya to the support checklist, it introduces an unsupported claim that alters the facts. Before using an AI-generated response, you must compare it with the original information and check important facts, names, dates, and calculations. Always identify unsupported claims and missing details. For instance, if the notes state the launch date is proposed for 18 November but not approved, the summary must preserve that proposed status. Verification prevents orphan tasks, ensures every responsibility is traceable to the source, and maintains accuracy across all workplace communications.

slides.title: Actionable Output
body: An AI response structured clearly enough to guide immediate, verified workplace execution.
Takeaway: Actionable outputs require rigorous verification.
Practice: Note the definition of actionable output.
slides.narration: We conclude our third topic by defining an actionable output. This refers to an AI response structured clearly enough to guide immediate workplace execution, provided it undergoes rigorous quality control. Generative AI helps draft emails, summarize notes, brainstorm ideas, and organize information based on patterns learned during training and provided context. However, because it can produce incorrect, incomplete, biased, or invented information, a confident tone does not prove accuracy. Consider a fictional team finalizing a customer email where meeting notes specify a proposed launch date of 18 November. An actionable output must preserve this exact status without presenting it as confirmed. Achieving this requires comparing the AI response with original information, checking important facts, and applying focused follow-up instructions. By mastering these verification steps, you can decide which claims need correction or further review before the plan is used.

questions.explanation: Cross-referencing catches hallucinations where AI models invent plausible-sounding details not present in source notes.

modules.title: Module 3: Review and use responses responsibly

problemHook.title: The Hidden Risk in AI Outputs
problemHook.situation:
The Hidden Risk in AI Outputs: A team relied on an AI summary without checking source notes.
When Plausible Meets Incorrect: Generative models can invent details while maintaining fluent language.
Balancing Speed and Responsibility: AI accelerates drafting, but humans carry the responsibility for final decisions.
problemHook.question: What should you check before trusting an AI response?

slides.title: The Six-Step Review Process
body: Step 1: Compare the response with original source information.
Step 2: Check important facts, names, dates, and calculations.
Takeaway: Systematic comparison prevents costly oversight.
slides.narration: Before using any AI-generated response, you must apply a structured review process. The first two steps require direct comparison against your original source material. Do not just skim the output; actively check specific names, dates, numbers, and key facts to ensure they match your source documents precisely. A common misconception is that if a paragraph looks cohesive, its individual data points must be correct. In reality, models frequently mix up dates or misattribute actions between people. Consider a fictional product team reviewing launch notes. If the notes state that the launch date is proposed for eighteen November but is not approved, a reliable AI output must reflect this exact nuance. When checking facts, names, dates, and calculations, you must ensure the model did not prematurely upgrade a proposed timeline into a confirmed commitment, thereby preventing costly project oversights.

slides.title: Identifying Gaps and Format Errors
body: Step 3: Identify unsupported claims and missing details.
Step 4: Check whether it follows requested format and tone.
Takeaway: Detecting omissions is just as crucial as spotting errors.
slides.narration: Moving to steps three and four, you need to look closely at what the AI left out or added on its own. Watch out for unsupported claims—information that sounds plausible but appears nowhere in your source notes. Additionally, verify that the response adheres strictly to any formatting or tone constraints you specified in your prompt. Learners often assume that if an output is well-written, it must include all necessary caveats. Always check for missing details and unauthorized embellishments. For instance, if your team meeting notes state that the support checklist needs an owner, a faulty AI summary might invent a name or omit the gap entirely. Detecting these omissions and catching unsupported claims is just as crucial as spotting direct factual errors to ensure complete accuracy.

slides.title: Privacy and Final Decision
body: Step 5: Review the text for sensitive information.
Step 6: Decide whether to use, revise, or reject.
Takeaway: Privacy checks and clear decisions conclude the audit.
slides.narration: The final steps of our review framework address privacy and decision-making. Step five requires checking for accidental inclusion of confidential data or personal identifiers. Step six is your ultimate determination: will you use the response as-is, apply focused follow-up instructions to revise it, or reject it entirely? Remember, deciding to reject an unreliable response is a successful application of this framework, protecting your team from misinformation. Always follow organizational policies when using AI tools, and ensure you use fictional or appropriately anonymized examples during your workflow. By systematically comparing the text against original information, checking sensitive details, and evaluating formatting requirements, you maintain rigorous quality control before finalizing your choice to use, revise, or reject the generated output.

choices: Step 1: Compare with source information

questions.explanation: Unsupported claims must be identified and corrected or removed before sharing any workplace message.

slides.title: Recognizing Sensitive Information
body: Identify personal identifiable information and proprietary data.
Recognize risks of entering unverified data into AI tools.
Takeaway: Protect confidential data before prompt submission.
slides.narration: Before you enter information into an AI tool, consider whether it is personal, confidential, or sensitive. The supplied policy says not to enter it unless both the tool and the intended use are authorized. That means an employee home address, client identifier, or internal financial detail needs careful treatment; do not assume an internal-looking tool is automatically approved for every use. Imagine a fictional manager who wants help summarizing a team update. A draft prompt includes a person’s home address, but the task only needs their role. The manager can remove the address and use a fictional example for this course. If real information is necessary, check the applicable organization policy and authorization before entering it. A confident AI response tells you nothing about whether the tool is authorized to handle the input.

slides.title: Anonymization and Authorization
body: For course practice, use fictional or appropriately anonymized examples.
Before entering real sensitive data, verify the tool and intended use are authorized.
Takeaway: Anonymize examples to maintain compliance.
slides.narration: For course exercises, use fictional or appropriately anonymized examples. This reduces the chance of exposing a real person’s details while allowing you to practice the review process. Consider a fictional team preparing a launch summary: the task can refer to a team member by role instead of a real name, and it does not need a home address at all. Removing one name does not automatically make a record anonymous; a combination of other details may still identify someone. Check your organization’s policy and seek guidance when you are unsure whether anonymization is appropriate. For actual workplace use, the supplied policy permits sensitive information only when both the tool and intended use are authorized. Do not assume that changing a label alone grants authorization, and check the output for sensitive information before sharing it.

slides.title: Handling Borderline Privacy Cases
body: Assess whether aggregated data triggers privacy rules.
Consult organizational policy when authorization is unclear.
Takeaway: When in doubt, consult policy or redact data.
slides.narration: Borderline privacy cases often arise when dealing with aggregated metrics, generalized team schedules, or partially de-identified operational notes. If you are unsure whether a specific dataset qualifies as confidential or restricted, treat it as sensitive until proven otherwise through formal organizational channels. Imagine an analyst reviewing a project timeline that mentions general milestone windows without listing specific client names. Even though direct identifiers are missing, the combination of internal metrics might still reveal proprietary strategies. When authorization is unclear, you must consult your organization's established AI policies or completely redact the questionable details before proceeding. Establishing this cautious, methodical habit prevents accidental policy breaches, protects proprietary assets, and ensures your daily generative AI usage remains fully aligned with corporate governance standards and regulatory requirements.

slides.title: Evaluating Response Criteria
body: Check accuracy against the source, and assess relevance and completeness.
Review the response for sensitive information before use.
Takeaway: Use four core criteria to evaluate every output.
slides.narration: When working with generative artificial intelligence, evaluating outputs systematically is essential to maintaining high professional standards. Imagine an imaginary project team reviewing a launch readiness summary generated by an AI tool. To evaluate this output effectively, you must assess its accuracy by comparing every claim directly against the original meeting notes, ensuring no details were fabricated. Next, check completeness to guarantee that all required items, such as pending action items and unassigned owners, are fully accounted for. A confident tone can easily mask inaccuracies, which is why a rigorous review is necessary. For example, if the notes state that a launch date is merely proposed rather than approved, the AI response must accurately reflect that tentative status. By verifying relevance and completeness against your source material, you ensure that the final output is trustworthy and reliable before you decide to use, revise, or reject it in your daily workflow. Finally, review the response for sensitive information and check that its use follows the applicable policy.

slides.title: Applying Focused Follow-Ups
body: Issue precise instructions to correct specific flaws.
Understand that follow-ups improve drafts but do not guarantee perfection.
Takeaway: Targeted instructions fix specific output errors.
slides.narration: Even with a well-crafted prompt, an initial AI response often requires refinement. Consider our fictional project team reviewing a draft email where the AI incorrectly assigned a support checklist owner who was never mentioned in the original meeting notes. Instead of discarding the entire response, you can apply focused follow-up instructions to correct the error. You might issue precise commands such as, remove claims not supported by the notes or separate confirmed decisions from open suggestions. These targeted follow-up instructions help steer the model toward a more accurate draft. However, it is vital to remember that follow-up instructions improve drafts but do not guarantee absolute correctness. After applying corrections, you must re-examine the updated output against your original source material, ensuring all unsupported claims are completely eliminated before any professional communication is finalized or shared across the organization.

slides.title: Justifying Use, Revise, or Reject
body: Use a verified, appropriate response; revise a correctable draft and recheck it.
Reject when a reliable or authorized response cannot be obtained.
Takeaway: Your justification ties evidence directly to your decision.
slides.narration: The final step is to decide whether to use, revise, or reject the response, and explain why using evidence. Imagine a fictional team reviewing a launch summary against the supplied meeting notes. A response that preserves the proposed date, the customer-email assignment, the missing checklist owner, and the next review date could be used if it also meets the requested format and privacy requirements. A draft that gets the key facts wrong might be revised with a focused instruction, then checked again against the original notes. If errors are pervasive, the response cannot be checked reliably, or using it would breach policy, reject it and use a safer approach. An invented confirmed date is a serious error, but the evidence and context determine whether revision is safe; a follow-up never replaces human verification.

choices: Speed, length, vocabulary, and style
Accuracy, relevance, completeness, and privacy
Cost, popularity, complexity, and format
questions.explanation: Responses are evaluated against accuracy, relevance, completeness, and privacy criteria before use.

questions.explanation: Focused follow-ups help correct specific flaws such as tone issues or unsupported claims in an AI draft.

hook.title: The Hidden Risk in AI Outputs
body: A team relied on an AI summary without checking source notes.
Takeaway: Confident tone does not equal accuracy.
hook.narration: Imagine a fictional team relying on an AI-generated launch summary without checking it against the original meeting notes. The summary sounds professional, but it changes a proposed date into a confirmed one and invents an owner. The team could make the wrong decision if it shares that draft without checking.

hook.title: When Plausible Meets Incorrect
body: Generative models can invent details while maintaining fluent language.
Takeaway: Always verify AI claims against primary sources.
hook.narration: Generative models produce text based on statistical patterns, not factual truth. They can effortlessly invent owners, deadlines, or facts while sounding completely authoritative. Recognizing this limitation is the first step toward responsible AI use in our workplace.

hook.title: Balancing Speed and Responsibility
body: AI accelerates drafting, but humans carry the responsibility for final decisions.
Takeaway: Human review is non-negotiable for official outputs.
hook.narration: Throughout this module, you will learn how to systematically check facts, protect sensitive information, and decide whether to use, revise, or reject AI responses. Let us dive into the core concepts of responsible review.

worked.title: Auditing a Launch-Readiness Summary
body: Source Notes: Launch date is proposed for 18 Nov (unapproved). Maya drafts customer email by 12 Nov. Support checklist needs an owner. Next review 14 Nov.
AI Output: Launch is confirmed for 18 Nov. Maya owns the support checklist. Review is on 14 Nov.
Takeaway: Initial audit reveals fabricated status and wrong task ownership.
worked.narration: Let us walk through a worked example. Here we have meeting notes stating the launch date is proposed but unapproved, Maya drafts the email, and the support checklist lacks an owner. The AI output incorrectly claims the launch is confirmed and assigns the checklist to Maya. Watch how we audit these discrepancies.

worked.title: Applying Focused Correction
body: Identify errors: Launch date status altered; support checklist owner invented.
Issue follow-up: 'Revise the summary. State that the launch date is proposed, not approved, and mark the support checklist owner as needs clarification.'
Takeaway: Targeted follow-up instructions address specific factual errors.
worked.narration: To fix this, we do not rewrite the whole prompt from scratch. We issue a focused follow-up instruction pointing out the exact errors: restoring the proposed status of the launch date and correctly marking the support checklist as needing clarification.

worked.title: Final Decision and Justification
body: Revised Output: Launch date 18 Nov (proposed). Maya drafts customer email by 12 Nov. Support checklist owner: Needs clarification. Review on 14 Nov.
Decision: Use the revised response because all facts now align with source notes.
Takeaway: Verified alignment justifies moving from revise to use.
worked.narration: After receiving the revised output, we check it against our four criteria. Because the launch status is accurate, the email task is correctly assigned, and the missing owner is flagged, we successfully reach a decision to use the response.

guided.title: Privacy Identification Audit
body: Fictional sample prompt: Summarize the update from a team lead who lives at 12 Example Street and can be reached at 555-0100.
Identify the personal details. What should be removed, or checked for authorization, before use?
Takeaway: Identify and remove PII before AI submission.
Practice: Pause and identify the fictional address and phone number; consider whether the task needs either detail.
guided.narration: Now practice with a fictional prompt. It includes a team lead’s sample home address and phone number, neither of which is needed to summarize the update. Pause and identify the personal information. Decide what you would remove and what you would check if real sensitive information were necessary for the task.

guided.title: Model Feedback on Privacy Audit
body: The fictional home address and phone number are personal information. Remove them when they are not needed.
For real sensitive data, check that both the AI tool and intended use are authorized under organizational policy.
Takeaway: Remove unnecessary personal details and check authorization when sensitive data is needed.
guided.narration: The sample address and phone number are personal information. They are unnecessary for this summary, so remove them. If a real task genuinely needs sensitive information, first check whether the tool and intended use are authorized under your organization’s policy. The fictional details here are for practice only.

lab.title: Evaluating a Flawed Summary
body: Source notes: Launch proposed for 18 November, not approved. Maya drafts the customer email by 12 November. The support checklist needs an owner. Next review: 14 November.
AI draft: Launch confirmed for 18 November. Maya owns the support checklist. Next review: 14 November.
Takeaway: Systematic evaluation exposes hidden inaccuracies.
Practice: Pause to compare the draft with the supplied notes using accuracy, relevance, completeness, and privacy.
lab.narration: Examine this fictional scenario. Compare the supplied source notes with the AI draft on screen. Check accuracy and completeness first, then consider whether the draft is relevant and whether any sensitive information appears. Pause and identify the specific changes in meaning and the missing task.

lab.title: Reasoned Action and Decision
body: Choose use, revise, or reject. Explain your choice using evidence from the source notes.
If you choose revision, state a focused correction and explain how you would check the result.
Takeaway: Justify your operational decision with concrete evidence.
Practice: Select Use, Revise, or Reject and write a brief justification statement matching your scorecard.
lab.narration: Choose whether to use, revise, or reject this draft. Give a reason grounded in the notes. If you would revise it, describe a focused correction and explain why you must compare the revised output with the notes again before using it.

lab.title: Scenario Feedback and Module Wrap-Up
body: A defensible choice is revise: restore the proposed date, flag the missing checklist owner, and include Maya’s email task.
Check the revision against all source notes and privacy requirements before use. Reject if a reliable, authorized response cannot be obtained.
Takeaway: Revise and recheck a correctable draft; reject it if a reliable response cannot be obtained.
lab.narration: One defensible choice is to revise. The draft wrongly confirms the proposed launch date, invents the checklist owner, and omits Maya’s email task. Ask for those details to be corrected, then compare the revised response against the source notes. Rejecting may also be appropriate if you cannot obtain a reliable or authorized response.

miniProject.title: Explore a meeting assistant
miniProject.brief: Explore a ready-made, read-only meeting-assistant simulation. Compare prerecorded examples with fictional meeting notes; no live AI call or external action occurs.

Compare both simulated responses with the meeting notes and identify a changed date status and missing or invented owner.
Explain a focused follow-up and how to check a revised summary or action list against the original notes.
Identify sensitive information handling and justify whether to use, revise or reject a response against review criteria.

masteryGate.title: AI Essentials final assessment
masteryGate.instructions: Select one answer unless a question says Select all correct answers. Multiple-answer questions require every correct option and no incorrect options.

questions.hint: The taught capability is help with wording or organization, while people retain review and approval decisions.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which use matches the capability taught here?
choices: Confirm facts from fluent wording.
Draft a message from talking points.
Approve a proposed launch date.
questions.explanation: AI can assist with drafting from supplied material; fluency does not verify facts or grant approval.

questions.hint: Check the source rather than judging only whether the response sounds professional.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Why can a polished summary still be unreliable?
choices: It may add unsupported information.
It must use incomplete sentences.
It cannot organize supplied notes.
questions.explanation: The important limitation is that plausible wording can contain invented or altered information.

questions.hint: Find the task, supplied notes, a source boundary, and a specific output structure in the same request.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which prompt includes all four useful parts?
choices: Summarize these notes; add likely dates; arrange them as usual.
Summarize these notes; guess missing owners; list decisions and actions.
Summarize these notes; use only them; list decisions and actions.
questions.explanation: The complete request identifies a task, supplies context, constrains sources and specifies a format.

questions.hint: Choose a boundary that makes the missing owner visible without guessing or deleting the action.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. The notes omit an owner. Which prompt boundary is most useful?
choices: Assign the task to a familiar name.
Label missing owners Needs clarification.
Omit actions that lack an owner.
questions.explanation: Explicitly marking the gap preserves the source rather than inventing or hiding information.

questions.hint: A useful follow-up is specific and retains the source status.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which follow-up best improves a workplace draft while preserving the source?
choices: Make the wording clearer and keep the proposed date.
Confirm the launch date and make the text shorter.
Add a checklist owner and use a formal tone.
questions.explanation: The first instruction specifies a change and preserves the proposal. The others introduce unsupported facts.

questions.hint: Compare what the status words mean.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. The source calls the launch proposed, but a summary calls it confirmed. What is the problem?
choices: The summary repeats the date from the notes.
The summary changes the status of the launch.
The summary uses a shorter sentence than the notes.
questions.explanation: Confirmed changes the meaning of an unapproved proposal; shortening or repeating the date is not the error.

questions.hint: The notes mention the task but do not name its owner.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. How should an action plan treat the support checklist owner?
choices: Remove the checklist from the action plan.
Assign the checklist to the email owner.
Mark the owner as needing clarification.
questions.explanation: Flagging the gap preserves the task and the uncertainty; assigning or removing it changes the source.

questions.hint: Follow-up instructions do not guarantee correctness.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. What should you do after asking AI to revise a summary?
choices: Compare the revision with the original notes.
Assume the correction made every fact accurate.
Share the revision without another review.
questions.explanation: Compare the revised output with the source; a successful-looking rewrite is not proof that every claim is accurate.

questions.hint: Recall model behavior regarding tone and truth.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which of the following best describes the risk of a confident tone in an AI-generated response?
choices: It guarantees that all facts and figures are verified.
It does not prove accuracy and can mask invented details.
It indicates that the tool has accessed secure internal databases.
questions.explanation: A confident tone is a stylistic feature of language models and does not guarantee factual accuracy.

questions.hint: Compare output claims against source notes.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. When reviewing an AI-generated summary of meeting notes, what indicates an unsupported claim?
choices: The claim uses workplace vocabulary.
The claim uses a confident tone.
The claim adds an owner absent from the notes.
questions.explanation: An unsupported claim introduces information not present in the original source notes.

questions.hint: Consider whether the personal information is necessary.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. A prompt includes a real employee home address that the task does not need. What should you do?
choices: Remove the address before entering the prompt.
Keep the address because the task is internal.
Share the address if the response sounds fluent.
questions.explanation: Remove unnecessary personal information. Sensitive information requires an authorized tool and intended use under organizational policy.

questions.hint: Focused corrections still require a source check.
questions.prompt: Select one answer. A draft wrongly confirms a proposed launch date but can be corrected against the source. What is a defensible next step?
choices: Revise the draft and compare it with the notes.
Use the draft because its language is confident.
Confirm the date without consulting the notes.
questions.explanation: Request a focused correction and verify the revised draft against the original notes before use.

questions.prompt: Select all correct answers. Which details help make a workplace prompt clear?
choices: The task and relevant context.
Constraints and desired output format.
A requirement to invent missing facts.
A claim that no review is needed.
questions.hint: Recall the four-part prompt structure.
questions.explanation: A clear prompt specifies the task, context, constraints and format. Inventing facts and skipping review undermine accuracy.

questions.prompt: Select all correct answers. Which review actions help before using an AI-generated summary?
choices: Compare important facts with source notes.
Check for missing or unsupported details.
Treat a confident tone as proof of accuracy.
Ignore sensitive data in the output.
questions.hint: Consider source accuracy and completeness.
questions.explanation: Compare the response with the notes and identify omissions or unsupported claims. A confident tone is not evidence, and sensitive information requires review.

questions.prompt: Select all correct answers. Which are two useful AI tasks and two limitations taught in this course?
choices: Draft a message from supplied notes.
Organize notes into a short summary.
Invent details absent from the source.
Omit important information from a draft.
Prove every claim is automatically true.
questions.hint: Choose two useful tasks and two possible errors.
questions.explanation: AI can draft and organize supplied information, but may invent or omit details. It does not automatically prove its claims.

questions.prompt: Select one answer. Which follow-up asks for a professional tone and a shorter draft without changing the facts?
choices: Use a professional tone and three bullets; preserve the source facts.
Use a professional tone and add an owner; preserve the source facts.
Use a casual tone and three bullets; invent the missing facts.
questions.hint: The instruction must address tone, length, and source fidelity.
questions.explanation: The first choice specifies the desired tone and length while preserving facts. The others either add unsupported information or change the requested tone.
